metadata.title: PISA 2015 Results (Volume IV): Students’ Financial Literacy

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This volume reports PISA 2015 results for the optional financial literacy assessment administered to 15-year-olds in participating countries and economies. The report uses PISA’s complex sampling design and provides weighted estimates for student- and school-level questionnaire responses (e.g., tables explicitly refer to weighted shares of students responding). The publication also describes how sampling and exclusion rates are controlled to keep distortions in national mean scores within a small range, and how uncertainty is quantified through sampling errors and standard errors. The document does not specify the exact weight variable names or replicate-weight method in the provided text excerpt, so the specific weight variable (e.g., a TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT-type field) and replicate procedure cannot be extracted here.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The financial literacy assessment in PISA 2015 was administered as an optional one-hour test comprising two clusters, delivered to a subsample of students in participating countries and economies. The target population is 15-year-olds (aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months) enrolled in school and having completed at least 6 years of formal schooling. The report applies PISA’s technical exclusion standards (e.g., overall exclusion rate required to remain below 5% in each country/economy under reasonable assumptions) and uses the PISA sampling design to obtain representative samples within each participating system. The excerpt does not provide further country-specific filtering beyond the financial literacy module being offered only in the listed participating countries/economies.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD volume reports PISA 2015 results for the optional domain of students’ financial literacy, assessed for 15-year-olds in participating countries and economies. The financial literacy assessment used a computer-based design and lasted one hour, consisting of two clusters administered to a subsample of students, while students also completed core PISA assessments (science, reading, mathematics) in the overall PISA design. Proficiency is reported on a financial literacy scale with five proficiency levels; Level 2 is identified as the baseline level of proficiency, and Level 5 as the highest. The report provides cross-country comparisons of mean performance and the distribution of students across proficiency levels, and it also describes relationships between financial literacy and student characteristics (e.g., socio-economic status, immigrant background, gender) and experiences with money (e.g., holding a bank account, discussing money with parents). It emphasizes that PISA cannot establish causal effects of policies or practices, and it highlights measurement and trend-interpretation considerations (e.g., changes in scaling and assessment administration between 2012 and 2015).
